scenes.visual: Title card 'One Synapse or Several' over a split screen: a leg kicking on the left, a foot lifting off a tack on the right. COLOUR MAP, same in both films and the lesson: the route is a GOLD line; five stations in fixed order and colours: receptor TEAL, sensory neuron BLUE, integrating centre in the spinal cord GREY, motor neuron ORANGE, effector muscle RED. A horizontal TIMER BAR at the bottom fills one segment per leg in the station colour (sensory BLUE, motor ORANGE), a short WHITE tick for each synapse, and a hatched GREY end block for junction and muscle. Inhibited muscles fade to pale grey. Numbers appear only as on-screen text. Cream background, 16:9. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'. Extensor muscles are the same RED as effectors; flexors are RED too; any inhibited muscle fades to pale grey.

scenes.tts: The first film timed the knee jerk, leg by leg. Now you step on a tack: is lifting your foot faster or slower, and why?
scenes.visual: The left panel replays the knee-jerk route in miniature with its filled timer bar from the first film. The right panel shows a bare foot coming down on a tack, then lifting. A question mark between the panels.
scenes.narration: The first film timed the knee jerk, leg by leg. Now you step on a tack: is lifting your foot faster or slower, and why?

scenes.tts: Put the two reflexes side by side. Both use the same five stations: receptor, sensory neuron, integrating centre, motor neuron, effector. Their circuits differ in the middle. Their fibres and path lengths differ too.
scenes.visual: Split screen, two human figures in side view, each with a GOLD route. Left: thigh spindle to cord and back. Right: sole of the foot to cord and back to flexor muscles of the thigh and lower leg. The same five coloured station labels sit under each. The GREY cord on each side zooms slightly larger.
scenes.narration: Put the two reflexes side by side. Both use the same five stations: receptor, sensory neuron, integrating centre, motor neuron, effector. Their circuits differ in the middle. Their fibres and path lengths differ too.

scenes.tts: In the knee jerk, the spindle's sensory fibre synapses straight onto the motor neuron. That is one synapse in the spinal cord. This direct path is called monosynaptic.
scenes.visual: Left cord, enlarged: a BLUE fibre enters and ends just short of an ORANGE motor neuron, with a narrow visible synaptic cleft between them; one WHITE tick flashes ('1 synapse'). Label 'monosynaptic'. The quadriceps glows RED.
scenes.narration: In the knee jerk, the spindle's sensory fibre synapses straight onto the motor neuron. That is one synapse in the spinal cord. This direct path is called monosynaptic.

scenes.tts: But a side branch excites an interneuron, a neuron that stays inside the cord. It quiets the hamstring, the muscle that would oppose the kick. So even the knee jerk is not one wire.
scenes.visual: A thin BLUE side branch reaches a small GREY interneuron (label 'interneuron'), which ends just short of a second ORANGE motor neuron across a narrow visible synaptic cleft marked with a minus sign. The hamstring at the back of the thigh fades to pale grey (label 'quieted').
scenes.narration: But a side branch excites an interneuron, a neuron that stays inside the cord. It quiets the hamstring, the muscle that would oppose the kick. So even the knee jerk is not one wire.

scenes.tts: Now the tack. Pain-sensing endings in the skin fire. Their thin sensory fibres excite a chain of interneurons in the cord, right from the start.
scenes.visual: Right panel: TEAL endings in the sole light up. A thinner BLUE fibre (drawn visibly thinner than the knee-jerk fibre) carries a pulse up the leg slowly. In the GREY cord it reaches a chain of two small GREY interneurons in series, so the path crosses three synapses: sensory to interneuron, interneuron to interneuron, interneuron to motor neuron.
scenes.narration: Now the tack. Pain-sensing endings in the skin fire. Their thin sensory fibres excite a chain of interneurons in the cord, right from the start.

scenes.tts: Some interneurons drive the flexors, which lift the foot. Others quiet the opposing extensors. Charles Sherrington showed this pairing in mammals, and called it reciprocal innervation.
scenes.visual: From the interneuron chain, ORANGE paths standing for pools of motor neurons go to the flexor muscles (glow RED, the knee and hip bend, the foot lifts); another path with a minus sign goes to the extensors, which fade to pale grey. Small caption: 'Sherrington: reciprocal innervation'.
scenes.narration: Some interneurons drive the flexors, which lift the foot. Others quiet the opposing extensors. Charles Sherrington showed this pairing in mammals, and called it reciprocal innervation.

scenes.tts: Now run both timers together, on the same scale. The withdrawal bar keeps growing after the knee jerk's has stopped. It has more synapses, so it shows more ticks.
scenes.visual: Two timer bars, one under each panel, start filling at the same moment and the same scale (computed illustrative model sum). Left: BLUE, one WHITE tick, ORANGE, hatched block. Right: a much longer BLUE segment, three WHITE ticks, a longer ORANGE segment, hatched block. The right bar keeps filling after the left has stopped.
scenes.narration: Now run both timers together, on the same scale. The withdrawal bar keeps growing after the knee jerk's has stopped. It has more synapses, so it shows more ticks.

scenes.tts: In this example the withdrawal has three synapses, and the knee jerk has only one. So are the extra synapses most of the extra time?
scenes.visual: Both full bars hold. The three WHITE ticks on the right bar pulse. Question mark.
scenes.narration: In this example the withdrawal has three synapses, and the knee jerk has only one. So are the extra synapses most of the extra time?

scenes.visual: Hold on the two full bars; the WHITE ticks pulse slowly.

scenes.tts: No. In this model, each synapse adds only about a millisecond. The big difference is the sensory leg. Thin pain fibres conduct slowly, so that leg takes tens of milliseconds.
scenes.visual: The bars split apart into their segments and line up by type. On-screen numbers (computed, illustrative): sensory 'knee 8.3 ms / withdrawal 45 ms'; synapses '1 ms / 3 ms'; motor '8.3 ms / 15 ms'; ends '1.5 ms / 1.5 ms'; totals 'about 19 ms / about 65 ms'. The BLUE sensory segment of the withdrawal bar glows; the tiny WHITE ticks sit small beside it.
scenes.narration: No. In this model, each synapse adds only about a millisecond. The big difference is the sensory leg. Thin pain fibres conduct slowly, so that leg takes tens of milliseconds.

scenes.tts: Why is a thin fibre slow? A thin axon offers more resistance to the current spreading ahead of the impulse. So the impulse travels more slowly, and the sensory leg stretches out.
scenes.visual: Two axon cartoons side by side, a wide BLUE one and a thin BLUE one, each with a pulse and a soft glow of current spreading ahead of it. The glow reaches far ahead in the wide axon and only a short way in the thin one; the thin axon's pulse lags behind. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Why is a thin fibre slow? A thin axon offers more resistance to the current spreading ahead of the impulse. So the impulse travels more slowly, and the sensory leg stretches out.

scenes.tts: Part of the gap is also the longer motor path. In this example, slow fibres are most of it, not all. In real people, fibre speed and processing in the cord both vary.
scenes.visual: A horizontal stacked bar labelled 'the extra time' splits into three coloured pieces (computed, model, rounded): BLUE 'slower sensory leg about 37 ms', ORANGE 'longer motor path about 7 ms', WHITE 'extra synapses 2 ms'. A faint dashed extension labelled 'real people: often near a tenth of a second (schematic)' runs beyond it.
scenes.narration: Part of the gap is also the longer motor path. In this example, slow fibres are most of it, not all. In real people, fibre speed and processing in the cord both vary.

scenes.tts: Both reflexes end on skeletal muscle, and that makes both of them somatic. Somatic does not mean voluntary. Neither reflex waits for a decision.
scenes.visual: Both panels return. The effector muscles in each glow RED with a label 'skeletal muscle → somatic'. A crossed-out speech bubble 'I decide' floats over each head.
scenes.narration: Both reflexes end on skeletal muscle, and that makes both of them somatic. Somatic does not mean voluntary. Neither reflex waits for a decision.

scenes.tts: So in these two reflexes, the synapses set the circuit. The slow fibres set most of the extra time. The sum from the first film still holds.
scenes.visual: The two routes collapse into one diagram: on the cord, a magnifier labelled 'synapses: the circuit'; on the BLUE and ORANGE axons, a ruler and stopwatch labelled 'fibres: most of the time (in these reflexes)'. The equation from the first film fades in beneath.
scenes.narration: So in these two reflexes, the synapses set the circuit. The slow fibres set most of the extra time. The sum from the first film still holds.

scenes.visual: End card with the Hex mascot holding a ruler and a stopwatch. Line: 'Here, slow fibres, not extra synapses, make most of the gap.'
